title: The final round
objectives: Plan a final-round day: pacing, recovering from a bad round and the questions to ask.

screens.title: A final-round day
screens.prose: Reported final days run three to five interviews (l4, October 2026). Nadia has four 45-minute rounds: probability at 9:30, market making at 10:30, coding at 11:30, behavioural at 13:30. Her market-making round goes badly.

state.caption: R1 to R4 are the four rounds, with lunch after R3.

screens.question: Drag Bad round onto the round that went badly.

hints.text: Which round starts at 10:30?
The second bar, R2, runs 10:30 to 11:15.
Drag the point onto R2.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Market making starts at 10:30.

byKey.bad: Drop the point on the 10:30 round, R2.

explain.text: Round 2 ran 10:30 to 11:15. Round 3 starts 15 minutes later, with a new interviewer. What she does in those 15 minutes decides how round 3 begins.

screens.prose: Round 2 is over. Each interviewer usually writes up their own round before the panel compares notes. A final-round plan has three parts: **pacing**, **recovering** and the **questions to ask**.
screens.question: How should Nadia treat round 3?

options.text: As a fresh start: a new interviewer marks it on its own
As practice, since the day is lost
options.why: You wrote off the day. One weak round among four is common, and the others still count.

options.text: Open by explaining what went wrong in round 2
options.why: You carried round 2 in. The new interviewer may know nothing about it.

options.text: As a round she must ace to make up for it
options.why: You raised the stakes. Pressing for perfect makes errors more likely.

hints.text: Who marks round 3?
A new interviewer, writing up only their own round.
Round 3 starts at zero.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Think about who marks round 3, and what they saw.

explain.text: Each round is usually marked on its own, so round 3 starts at zero. Recovering is the second part of the plan, and it starts in the gap. The other two parts are pacing within a round and the questions you ask.

screens.prose: Recovering. The 15 minutes before round 3 hold a 60-second reset. Put Nadia's reset in order.
screens.question: Order the reset. Leave out the step that does not belong.

lines.text: Write one line on paper about what to fix
Put the note away and turn to round 3
Replay the mistake in your head to learn from it now
lines.why: You kept the replay. It carries round 2 into round 3; learn from it tonight.

hints.text: Body first, then the lesson, then forward.
Water and a breath can go either way round.
Water, breath, one line, put it away. Leave out the replay.

feedback.correct: Settle, park the lesson, move on.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. End the reset facing round 3.

byKey.replay: You kept the replay. Reliving round 2 now spends the gap and carries it into round 3.
byKey.left-out: You left out a step that belongs. Only the replay goes.

explain.text: Water and a breath settle the body. One written line parks the lesson so the mind can let go. The full replay waits until the evening, when it costs nothing.

screens.prose: Pacing within a round. In round 3, Nadia has just answered the first question in about four minutes.

lines: Interviewer: Two cards from a shuffled deck. Chance both are aces?
You: First ace 4/52, then 3/51, so 12/2652, which is 1/221.
You: Check: small, as it should be; about 0.45%.

screens.question: What should she say next?

options.text: "Would you like me to go further, or move on?"
Talk through a second method, unasked
options.why: You kept going unasked. It spends the round on a question already answered.

options.text: Stay silent and wait for the next question
options.why: You waited silently. Offering depth hands the interviewer the choice.

options.text: "I'm not sure that's right, though."
options.why: You undercut a checked answer. If you have a doubt, name it precisely.

hints.text: Who should choose what happens next?
The answer is given and checked in lines 2 and 3.
Offer more depth, and let the interviewer decide.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Hand the interviewer the next choice.

explain.text: Answer, check, then offer depth: that keeps the round at the interviewer's pace. They may want a harder version or the next question. Either way, you have not spent time they wanted elsewhere.

screens.prose: Round 4 is behavioural. The interviewer asks: "Tell me about a time you had to make a call without all the facts." Here are Nadia's six stories from l11.

rows: Momentum test; found a look-ahead bug in my own code
52% against a 70% aim; new revision plan; 71% in June
Trading game; chose half size with data missing; argued for it
Captain; talked the team into a new plan; won 6 of 8 after
Disagreed with the manager; used sales data; waste £120 to £70
Took over accounts, never kept any, 2 weeks before a tournament

screens.question: Which story should she tell?

options.text: The trading game: half size with data missing
The netball plan
options.why: You picked a team and persuasion story. No facts were missing in it.

options.text: The probability exam
options.why: You picked the failure story. There was no call to make on missing facts.

options.text: A new story made up to fit
options.why: You made one up. Follow-up questions expose invented detail.

hints.text: Which story has a decision with something unknown?
Look for "data missing".
The trading game.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Match the question to the story built for it.

explain.text: The trading-game story was built for this question: a decision with data missing. In a final round the six stories do the same job as in a recorded video. Pick, note three words, and answer.

screens.prose: Each round ends with "Any questions for me?" Sort Nadia's six questions. Intern work: "What do interns own?" Feedback: "How is feedback given?" Surprises: "What surprised you here?" What it does: "What does the firm do?"

state.caption: Drag each card to Ask or Do not ask.

screens.question: Sort the six cards into Ask and Do not ask.

hints.text: Which questions are about the work and the person?
Pay and hours are for the recruiter, after an offer.
Ask: intern work, feedback, surprises. Do not ask: bonus, hours, what it does.

feedback.correct: Three to ask, three to leave.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Keep the questions about the work and how you would learn.

byKey.bonus: Pay questions belong with the recruiter, once you hold an offer.
byKey.hours: Hours belong with the recruiter after an offer, or with interns you meet.
byKey.what: Asking what the firm does shows no research. You should know before the day.
byKey.own: What interns own is about the work itself. Ask it.
byKey.fb: How feedback is given tells you how you would learn. Ask it.
byKey.sur: What surprised them invites a real, personal answer. Ask it.

explain.text: Good questions are about the work, how you learn and the person in front of you. Pay and hours are fair questions for the recruiter once you hold an offer. "What does the firm do?" tells the interviewer you did not look.

screens.prose: Round 3 begins. The new interviewer says hello and asks how the day is going.

rows: "Honestly, round 2 went badly, so sorry in advance."
"Fine. Can we go straight to the question?"

screens.question: What should she say?

options.text: "Good, thanks. I'm enjoying the problems."
"Honestly, round 2 went badly, so sorry in advance."
options.why: You apologised for round 2.

options.text: "Fine. Can we go straight to the question?"
options.why: You cut the greeting short. A curt start reads as tension.

hints.text: What does this interviewer know about round 2?
Probably nothing yet.
A short, true, positive answer.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Start round 3 at zero.

byKey.sorry: You apologised for round 2 at the start of round 3. This interviewer had no view of it, and now expects a weak round.
byKey.curt: You rushed the greeting. It shows the tension you are carrying from round 2.

explain.text: The round 3 interviewer starts with no view of round 2. An apology hands them a doubt they did not have. A short, true, positive answer starts the round at zero.

screens.prose: An edge case. In round 4 the interviewer asks a question Nadia solved last week, in practice.

lines: Interviewer: A stick is broken at two random points. Chance the three pieces make a triangle?

screens.question: What should she do?

options.text: "I've seen this one before. Let me solve it anyway, step by step."
Pretend it is new and act out working it out
options.why: You pretended. Interviewers often spot a too-smooth answer, and honesty is marked.

options.text: Ask for a different question instead
options.why: You refused it. Saying you have seen it, then solving it, shows honesty and method.

options.text: Give the answer, 1/4, at once with no working
options.why: You recited the answer. The method is what is marked.

hints.text: What is being marked: the number or the method?
Honesty is marked too.
Say you have seen it, then solve it aloud.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Be honest, and still show the method.

explain.text: Saying you have seen it is honest, and interviewers report marking honesty. They may give you a harder version, which is a chance to shine. Pretending is usually found out by a follow-up.

screens.prose: Why plan a recovery at all? If each round goes badly with chance $p$, independently, $$P(\text{at least one bad round}) = 1 - (1 - p)^n$$ With $p = 0.2$ and four rounds that is $1 - 0.8^4 \approx 0.59$.
screens.question: With five rounds, what is the chance of at least one bad round?

hints.text: Find the chance that no round goes badly first.
Each round is fine with chance 0.8.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Take 1 minus the chance that all five go well.

byKey.one: You gave one round's chance. There are five rounds.
byKey.added: You added the chances: 5 × 0.2 = 1. That counts days with two bad rounds twice.
byKey.none: That is the chance that no round goes badly. Take it from 1.

explain.text: $1 - 0.8^5 = 1 - 0.328 = 0.672$. On a five-round day a bad round is more likely than not, so plan for it. The 0.2 is an illustration, not a reported rate.

screens.prose: Some final rounds are on video. The same plan holds, with a few changes for the room.

rows: At eye level, face lit from in front
Quiet, door shut, phone in a drawer
A pad and pen within reach
The recruiter's number, in case the link drops

screens.question: Select all that apply: which set-ups help a remote final round?

options.text: Camera at eye level, face lit
A quiet room, phone away
Paper and pen within reach
The recruiter's number for a dropped link
Notes open on a second screen
options.why: You kept notes on screen. Your eyes drift, and some firms do not allow it.

options.text: Laptop on battery only
options.why: You left it unplugged. A long day can drain it mid-round.

hints.text: What does the interviewer need to see and hear?
Paper matters: you will work problems.
Camera, room, paper, backup. Not notes on screen or battery only.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Keep what makes you clear, calm and reachable.

explain.text: Remote rounds need a lit face, a quiet room, paper, and the recruiter's number for a dropped link. Notes on a second screen pull your eyes off the camera. Check the invitation for what is allowed.

screens.prose: **Follow-up.** Nadia asks "What do interns own?" The interviewer answers, then turns it round. Pace: about 30 seconds.

lines: You: What do interns own here?
Interviewer: One project each, start to finish. What would you want to own?

screens.question: Which reply is strongest?

options.text: "A pricing tool for one product, like my dice simulator but tested on real data."
"Anything; I'm happy to help wherever."
options.why: You gave no preference. The question invites you to link your evidence to the work.

options.text: "A new trading strategy for the whole desk."
options.why: You aimed too high. An intern project is small and finished.

options.text: "I'm not sure yet."
options.why: You stopped. Name one thing, even tentatively.

hints.text: What evidence does Nadia already have?
Her CV has a dice market simulator.
Link it to one small, finishable project.

feedback.correct: Her evidence, linked to a small project.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Pick the reply that links something she has done to the work.

explain.text: Every question you ask can come back to you. A strong reply links one piece of your evidence to a project an intern could finish. Prepare a short answer for each question you plan to ask.

screens.prose: Your own checklist for the day before a final round. Put Nadia's in order, from morning to night. Leave out the step that does not belong. You write your own final-round plan in homework 3.

state.caption: Her day: four rounds and lunch.

screens.question: Order the checklist. Leave out the step that does not belong.

lines.text: Confirm the time, and the address or video link
Print two copies of your CV
Write the six story cue words on a card
Write two questions for each round
Start a new puzzle book that evening
lines.why: You kept the new puzzle book. A hard new problem the night before costs sleep and confidence.

hints.text: What must be fixed while there is still time?
Logistics first, sleep last; the middle three can go in any order.
Confirm, then CVs, cues and questions, then sleep. Leave out the puzzle book.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Fix what could go wrong first, and end with sleep.

byKey.puzzle: You kept the new puzzle book. The evening before is for rest, not new problems.
byKey.left-out: You left out a step that belongs. Only the puzzle book goes.

explain.text: Logistics come first, while there is time to fix a wrong address. Materials and cues are prepared once, so the morning holds no surprises. The night is for sleep, not new problems.

ideas: Plan a final day in three parts: pacing in each round, recovering between rounds, and questions to ask.
Each round starts at zero: reset in 60 seconds, and never carry a bad round into the next.
Ask about the work and how you will learn; leave pay and hours for the recruiter after an offer.

formula.name: Expect a bad round
formula.note: With p = 0.2 and four rounds, about 0.59.

summary.trap: Apologising for a bad round at the start of the next one.

quiz.question: Round 1 went badly. What do you do in the 15-minute gap?

options.text: Water, one breath, one written line, then turn to round 2
Replay round 1 to find every mistake
options.why: You replayed it. That carries round 1 into round 2.

options.text: Email the recruiter to explain
options.why: You explained mid-day. It draws attention to a round that may not matter.

options.text: Revise round 1's topic in a hurry
options.why: You crammed. Fifteen minutes cannot change your knowledge, only your state.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Use the gap to arrive fresh.

explain.text: The gap is for your state, not your knowledge. A 60-second reset parks round 1 and starts round 2 at zero.

quiz.question: Which question is best to ask an interviewer?

options.text: "How do interns get feedback on their work?"
"What is the starting bonus?"
options.why: You asked about pay. Save it for the recruiter, after an offer.

options.text: "What does the firm trade?"
options.why: You asked what you should already know.

options.text: "Did I pass the last round?"
options.why: You asked for a verdict. The interviewer cannot give one.

feedback.correct: A question about how you would learn.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask about the work or how you would learn.

explain.text: Questions about the work and feedback show interest and give you real information. Pay, basics and verdicts do not.

quiz.question: Each of three rounds goes badly with chance 0.1, independently. What is the chance of at least one bad round?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Take 1 minus the chance that all three go well.

byKey.added: You added 0.1 three times. That counts two bad rounds twice.
byKey.none: That is the chance of no bad round. Take it from 1.

explain.text: $1 - 0.9^3 = 1 - 0.729 = 0.271$. As a check, it is a little under $3 \times 0.1$, because adding counts overlaps twice.

quiz.question: An interviewer asks a puzzle you have practised before. What do you do?

options.text: Say you have seen it, then solve it aloud
Pretend it is new
options.why: You pretended. A too-smooth answer is often noticed.

options.text: Give the answer at once
options.why: You recited. The method is what is marked.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Be honest, then show the working.

explain.text: Honesty is marked, and the method still has to be shown. You may get a harder version, which is a chance to do well.
